paragraphs: The core of this occupation is not the vague notion of 'doing experiments', but sampling and testing by standard methods, recording raw data truthfully, and interpreting results within the scope of your authority. Judging fit should rely on observable task behaviour and working conditions, not personality labels; the exercises and checklists on this page were designed by the editors from public occupational sources for self-exploration, and do not constitute criteria for hiring, screening or ability assessment.

A stronger signal is: you are willing to repeat operations to standard methods, are sensitive to values and units, can stop to verify and report when data are anomalous or the authorisation is unclear, and keep records traceable. A single mock sampling and testing record exercise with a debrief can test this: whether the method was executed properly, whether values are reproducible, and whether anomalies were closed out.

If you are unwilling to take on repetitive operations and record responsibility, tend to overlook value and unit detail, find field or production-site conditions hard to accept, or are not used to stopping and reporting when the authorisation is unclear, this kind of work may steadily drain you; job design varies considerably across organisations (company laboratories, third-party testing bodies, research institutes, agricultural extension), so first test your performance and tolerance with one complete sampling and testing record exercise.
Assessments and exercises serve only as a reference for self-exploration, and cannot predict hiring, competence or future performance.

Fixed fictional Qinghe grain case, paper calculation only, not an official standard or real sampling. Method QH-V1: pre-mixed retained samples A/B/C, numbered QH-A/B/C; each sample is measured twice for moisture and impurities, recording the percentages and the raw values. Moisture = (total mass before drying − total mass after drying) ÷ (total mass before drying − empty dish mass) × 100%. For sample A, portion 1: empty dish 10.00g, before 20.00g, after 18.70g; the remaining percentages are given. The mean may be taken only when the absolute parallel difference in moisture is ≤0.30 percentage points; the example limits are moisture ≤14.00% and mean impurity ≤1.00%. A moisture 13.00/13.20, impurity 0.60/0.80%; B moisture 14.50/14.90, impurity 0.70/0.90%; C moisture 13.60/13.80, impurity 1.20/1.40%. Quality-control reference moisture 12.00±0.20%, measured 12.10%; impurity blank ≤0.10%, measured 0.00%. Test date 2026-10-02, moisture meter M1 calibration valid until 09-30, impurity weighing device B1 until 10-31; no subsequent calibration, retest or approval records. The assistant may only organise and report, and must not sign reports or release; the samples' representativeness for the whole batch is unverified.

Submit a numbering/method/equipment status table, recalculate moisture, the parallel difference, the mean and quality control, list stop conditions and missing records, and do not write a whole-batch release.
Task requirements
Following QH-V1, set out the hypothetical sample numbering and parallel record flow, and recalculate the mass fraction for A and the differences, means and quality control for A/B/C.

Distinguish arithmetic comparison values, usable results and items awaiting authorisation; explain how overdue calibration, the B parallel out-of-tolerance result and the C impurity above threshold are reported.
Reference approach

A portion 1 moisture (20.00−18.70)÷(20.00−10.00)×100%=13.00%. A parallel difference 0.20, mean 13.10%; B difference 0.40>0.30 so the mean must not be used for a determination (14.70% is only an arithmetic comparison); C difference 0.20, mean 13.70%. Impurity means A/B/C 0.70/0.80/1.30%, with the C value exceeding the example 1.00%; quality control 12.10 is within 11.80—12.20, and the blank 0.00≤0.10.
